speaker: Doctor
text: How long have you had this painful, ulcerative lesion on your leg, and has it spread or changed in appearance since it started?

speaker: Patient
text: 54-year-old woman. The patient reports a skin lesion on her right leg that has been present for 1 month. The lesion began as a small red spot and has increased in size. She recalls an ant bite at the site before the lesion developed. She has a history of anterior uveitis treated with corticosteroids 8 months ago, as well as Crohn's disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and hypertension.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Has the lesion developed any nodules, purpura, or a "violaceous" (purple) border, and does it tend to appear in crops on your legs?

REQUEST TEST: Complete Blood Count (CBC), Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR), and C-Reactive Protein (CRP).
REQUEST IMAGES: Close-up clinical photograph of the leg lesion.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Complete Blood Count (CBC): Normal WBC, Normal Hemoglobin, Normal Platelets; Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR): Not available in provided data; C-Reactive Protein (CRP): Not available in provided data. Clinical Observation: The lesion presents with purplish irregular borders consistent with the patient's description of a violaceous border; no mention of discrete nodules or crops in the provided data. Skin Biopsy Histopathology: Neutrophilic infiltration without infection, consistent with pyoderma gangrenosum.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Pyoderma Gangrenosum. Given your history of Crohn's disease and the clinical presentation of a painful ulcer with violaceous borders and neutrophilic infiltration, this is a classic case of pyoderma gangrenosum, likely associated with your underlying inflammatory bowel disease. We should avoid debridement as it can worsen the lesion ("pathergy") and instead initiate systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressants.
